Fundamental Economic Concepts: The study of how people allocate limited resources to unlimited wants
The basic problem that resources are limited but wants are not
The value of the next best alternative given up by a choice
Giving up some of one thing to get more of another
The skills, knowledge, and experience workers bring to production
Weighing the additional benefit against the additional cost of one more unit
Something that motivates a person to act a certain way
A graph showing the maximum combinations an economy can produce
Producing the most output possible from available resources
Supply and Demand: Demand
The quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase at each price
Law of demand
As price rises, quantity demanded falls
Supply
The quantity producers are willing to offer at each price
Law of supply
As price rises, quantity supplied rises
Equilibrium price
The price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
Surplus
Excess supply when price sits above equilibrium
Shortage
Excess demand when price sits below equilibrium
Substitute good
A product bought instead of another, like tea for coffee
Complementary good
A product bought alongside another, like printers and ink
Elasticity of demand
How much quantity demanded responds to a price change
Price ceiling
A legal maximum price, which can create shortages
Price floor
A legal minimum price, which can create surpluses
Market Structures: Perfect competition
Many small firms selling identical products with free entry
Monopoly
A single seller controlling an entire market
Oligopoly
A market dominated by a few large firms
Monopolistic competition
Many firms selling similar but differentiated products
Barrier to entry
An obstacle making it hard for new firms to enter a market
Product differentiation
Making a product seem distinct from competitors
Price maker
A firm with enough power to set its own price
Price taker
A firm that must accept the market price
Antitrust law
Legislation preventing monopolies and promoting competition
Natural monopoly
A market where one firm can supply most cheaply, such as utilities
Collusion
Firms secretly cooperating to fix prices, generally illegal
Cartel
A formal agreement among producers to limit output and raise prices
Business Organizations: Sole proprietorship
A business owned by one person with unlimited personal liability
Partnership
A business owned by two or more people sharing profits and liability
Corporation
A business that is a separate legal entity from its owners
Limited liability
Owners risk only what they invested, not personal assets
Stock
A share representing partial ownership of a corporation
Dividend
A share of profits paid out to stockholders
Franchise
A licence to operate a business using another company's brand and system
Cooperative
A business owned and run by the members it serves
Nonprofit organization
An organisation whose surplus funds its mission rather than owners
Double taxation
Corporate profits taxed once as income and again as dividends
Labor and Wages: Labor force
Everyone employed or actively seeking work
Unemployment rate
The share of the labour force without a job and seeking one
Frictional unemployment
Short-term joblessness while moving between jobs
Structural unemployment
Joblessness from a mismatch of skills and available work
Cyclical unemployment
Joblessness caused by a downturn in the business cycle
Minimum wage
The legal lowest hourly pay an employer may offer
Labor union
A worker organisation bargaining collectively over pay and conditions
Collective bargaining
Negotiation between a union and an employer
Derived demand
Demand for labour that comes from demand for the product it makes
Productivity
Output produced per hour of work
Money and Banking: Money
Anything widely accepted as payment for goods and services
Medium of exchange
Money's function as an accepted means of payment
Store of value
Money's function of holding purchasing power over time
Unit of account
Money's function as a common measure of value
Fiat money
Currency with value by government declaration rather than commodity backing
Commercial bank
A financial institution accepting deposits and making loans
Fractional reserve banking
Banks keeping only part of deposits and lending the rest
Interest
The cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving it
Federal Reserve
The central bank of the United States
FDIC
Agency insuring bank deposits so savers do not lose money in a bank failure
Liquidity
How easily an asset can be converted to cash
Credit
The ability to borrow now and repay later
Government and the Economy: A good that is non-excludable and non-rival, such as national defence
A cost or benefit affecting someone not involved in the transaction
A spillover cost imposed on others, such as pollution
A spillover benefit to others, such as vaccination
A government payment supporting a business or activity
Government rules constraining how businesses operate
A tax taking a larger percentage from higher incomes
A tax taking a larger percentage from lower incomes
When a market on its own allocates resources inefficiently
Fiscal and Monetary Policy: Fiscal policy
Government use of taxing and spending to influence the economy
Expansionary fiscal policy
Cutting taxes or raising spending to stimulate growth
Contractionary fiscal policy
Raising taxes or cutting spending to slow inflation
Monetary policy
Central bank control of money supply and interest rates
Open market operations
The Fed buying or selling government bonds to shift the money supply
Discount rate
The interest rate the Fed charges banks for short-term loans
Reserve requirement
The share of deposits banks must hold rather than lend
Federal funds rate
The overnight rate banks charge each other, the Fed's main lever
Budget deficit
Spending exceeding revenue within a year
National debt
The accumulated total of past deficits
Crowding out
Government borrowing raising rates and reducing private investment
Multiplier effect
One round of spending generating further rounds of income
Measuring the Economy: Gross domestic product
The total market value of goods and services produced in a year
Real GDP
GDP adjusted for inflation, allowing comparison across years
Nominal GDP
GDP measured at current prices, unadjusted for inflation
GDP per capita
GDP divided by population, a rough measure of living standards
Inflation
A general rise in prices that reduces purchasing power
Deflation
A general fall in prices, often a sign of economic weakness
Consumer Price Index
A measure of price change in a typical basket of goods
Business cycle
The pattern of expansion, peak, contraction, and trough
Recession
A significant decline in economic activity lasting months
Standard of living
The level of material comfort available to a population
International Trade: Absolute advantage
Producing more of a good than another country with the same resources
Comparative advantage
Producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
Specialization
Concentrating on producing what you make most efficiently
Free trade
Trade without tariffs, quotas, or other barriers
Protectionism
Shielding domestic industry from foreign competition
Quota
A limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
Embargo
A ban on trade with a particular country
Balance of trade
The difference between a country's exports and imports
Exchange rate
The price of one currency expressed in another
Trade deficit
Importing more in value than a country exports
Economic Development: Developed country
A nation with high income, industry, and living standards
Developing country
A nation with lower income and less industrialisation
Infrastructure
The roads, power, water, and networks an economy runs on
Foreign direct investment
Investment by a company into operations in another country
Microfinance
Very small loans supporting entrepreneurship in poor communities
Sustainable development
Growth that does not exhaust resources for future generations
Brain drain
The emigration of skilled workers from a developing country
Literacy rate
The share of the population able to read and write
Life expectancy
Average lifespan, used as an indicator of development
Human Development Index
A composite measure of income, education, and health
Personal Finance and Economics: A plan matching expected income against planned spending
A recurring cost that stays the same, such as rent
A cost that changes month to month, such as groceries
Take-home pay after taxes and deductions
Interest earned on both the principal and prior interest
A number summarising how reliably someone repays debt
The original amount borrowed or invested
Savings set aside to cover unexpected costs
The principle that higher potential returns carry higher risk
